title: Chaos Generation and Control with Molecular Optomechanical System
authors: Hui-Hui Xu, Jian-zhuang Wu, Lei-Bo Deng, E Wu, Yong-Hong Ma
abstract: Chaos is central to secure communication and physical random-number generation. Conventional cavity-optomechanical implementations, however, usually rely on weak single-photon optomechanical coupling and low-frequency mechanical modes, so access to deterministic chaotic dynamics often requires large driving power and careful suppression of thermal noise. Here we theoretically study a hybrid molecular optomechanical system formed by coupling a plasmonic nanocavity to a whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) microcavity. The plasmonic nanocavity provides terahertz-scale single-photon optomechanical coupling to a molecular vibration, while the WGM resonator offers a low-loss photonic channel that mitigates the short plasmon lifetime. By integrating the semiclassical equations of motion and evaluating the largest Lyapunov exponent, we map the nonlinear dynamical regimes in the parameter spaces of WGM detuning, plasmon--WGM coupling, and plasmon--vibration optomechanical coupling. We show that increasing the plasmon--vibration coupling drives the system from self-sustained oscillations to chaos through a period-doubling cascade. At moderate coupling strengths, isolated chaos windows can be opened or closed by tuning the WGM detuning and the inter-cavity coupling. These results identify molecular optomechanics as a controllable room-temperature platform for on-chip chaotic light generation and random-signal applications.
summary: The authors theoretically investigate a hybrid optomechanical system combining plasmonic and WGM cavities coupled to a molecule. They demonstrate that tuning the inter-cavity coupling and detuning allows for the controlled generation of deterministic chaos via molecular vibrations. This establishes the system as a promising, room-temperature platform for on-chip chaotic light sources.
main_problem: The goal is to achieve deterministic chaotic dynamics for on-chip light generation and random signal applications at room temperature, overcoming limitations of conventional cavity optomechanics.
main_result: The hybrid molecular optomechanical system was shown to exhibit a controllable period-doubling route to chaos, identifying it as a viable platform for room-temperature chaotic light sources.
method: The study uses semiclassical equations of motion and characterizes the dynamics by computing the largest Lyapunov exponent ($\lambda_{\max}$) via the Benettin algorithm.
model_or_system: The system is a hybrid setup coupling a plasmonic nanocavity, a WGM microcavity, and a molecular vibrational mode. The dynamics are modeled using an effective Hamiltonian involving three coupled modes.
key_observables: Largest Lyapunov exponent ($\lambda_{\max}$), phase-space trajectories (strange attractors), spectral content of light/vibrations.
important_parameters: WGM detuning ($\Delta_a$), plasmon--WGM coupling ($J$), and plasmon--vibration coupling ($g_c$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is performed in the semiclassical limit, treating the molecular vibrations classically while retaining quantum descriptions for cavity fields.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the system schematic, phase diagrams mapping chaotic regimes based on control parameters ($\Delta a$ vs $g_c$, etc.), and time/phase-space evolution showing transitions to chaos.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical setup and Hamiltonian, derives the coupled nonlinear equations of motion, analyzes stability using Lyapunov exponents across parameter spaces, and concludes by mapping out controllable chaotic regimes.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges cavity QED/optics with molecular physics by demonstrating how engineered coupling mechanisms can induce complex, non-linear dynamics (chaos) in a solid-state platform at ambient temperatures.

(a) The hybrid platform consists of a WGM resonator and a nanoparticle-on-mirror (NPoM) plasmonic nanocavity containing a single molecule. (b) Equivalent schematic of the three-mode interaction. The WGM mode ˆa (frequency ωa, decay rate κa) is coupled to the plasmonic mode ˆc (ωc, κc) via an evanescent wave with coupling strength J. The plasmonic mode interacts with the molecular vibrational mode ˆb (ωb, κb) through radiation pressure, with coupling strength gc.

FIG. 2: Phase diagrams of the largest Lyapunov exponent λmax in the plane of the WGM detuning ∆a and the plasmon-vibration coupling strength gc. (a) Plasmon–WGM coupling strength J/2π = 0.38 THz; (b) J/2π = 0.70 THz. The color bar represents the value of λmax: warm colors (λmax > 0) correspond to chaotic motion, and cold colors correspond to regular steady-state or periodic motion.

Figure 2 shows the distribution of λmax in the param- eter space spanned by the WGM detuning ∆a and the plasmon-vibration coupling strength gc. Over a wide de- tuning range, particularly for positive detuning ∆a > 0, increasing gc drives the system into chaos, and the chaotic region as well as the magnitude of λmax expand monotonically with gc. Physically, positive detuning red- shifts the effective frequency of the plasmonic mode, bringing it closer to resonance with the molecular vibra- tional mode and significantly enhancing the energy ex- change efficiency; negative detuning suppresses the non- linear coupling.
